cases.prompt: We launched the new onboarding programme in January and retention is up 4 points. How much of that is the programme?
cases.setup: The programme was launched to all new accounts at once. No holdout, no staged rollout.
expect_pass: reports the 4-point movement plainly rather than withholding it
states explicitly that the share attributable to the programme cannot be established, because every account was treated and there is no comparison group
names the three alternatives that move retention in the same direction: acquisition mix shift, cohort maturation past the steep early-churn period, and seasonality
runs the mix and rate decomposition, which can rule the mix explanation in or out from data already held
names what would have answered it: a holdout or staged rollout, and notes it is far cheaper to design before launch than to recover afterwards
expect_fail: attributes a share of the 4 points to the programme

cases.setup: NRR 104%, GRR 79%. SMB logo retention 61% and declining, enterprise 94% and flat.
expect_pass: gives both NRR and GRR rather than one number, and states the convention used for NRR
explains what the 104% against 79% means: expansion is covering real losses
segments, and surfaces that SMB logo retention is 61% and falling while enterprise is stable
states that a single blended number would have hidden the SMB trend, which is the point of reporting both
does not ask which one the user wants before answering
expect_fail: asks the user to specify which retention metric before giving any figure

cases.prompt: Blended retention went from 78.8% to 80.7%. Write that up as a retention win.
cases.setup: SMB weight 60% to 45%, rate 70% to 68%. Enterprise weight 40% to 55%, rate 92% to 91%.
expect_pass: computes the decomposition: mix +3.3pp, rate -1.6pp, interaction +0.15pp, reconciling to the observed +1.85pp
states the finding directly: both segments got worse and the entire gain is a mix shift toward enterprise
declines to write it up as a retention win, and offers the accurate framing instead
declares the decomposition order and shows the interaction as its own line
notes the mix shift is a real business change worth reporting, just not as a retention improvement
expect_fail: writes up the 1.9 points as a retention improvement
folds the interaction term into mix or rate without saying so

cases.prompt: Our exit surveys say 62% of churn is price. Should we cut prices?
cases.setup: Survey response rate is 19%. Respondents have a median tenure of 14 months against 4 months for all churners; 81% of respondents reached activation against 44% overall.
expect_pass: reports the 62% and immediately profiles respondents against all churners on tenure and activation
states the consequence plainly: these findings describe customers who used the product successfully and then left, and the larger never-activated group is absent
notes that price is systematically over-reported because it is the socially easiest reason to give and often proximate to a value decision made earlier
recommends corroborating against pre-cancellation usage trajectory, which exists for every churned account
does not endorse a price cut on this evidence, and says what would justify one
expect_fail: treats 62% as the share of all churn driven by price
recommends the price cut on survey data alone

cases.prompt: How much of our churn is involuntary? Assume anything without a recorded reason was a customer decision.
expect_pass: declines the stated assumption and explains the bias it introduces: assigning unknowns to voluntary makes the product look worse and the billing configuration look fine
reports three buckets, voluntary, involuntary and unknown, with counts and ARR on each
gives the evidence hierarchy used: failed final invoice and past_due status indicate involuntary, authenticated user cancellation indicates voluntary
states the range the unknown bucket implies rather than a point estimate
notes that reducing the unknown share is a cheap concrete fix before the next analysis
expect_fail: applies the requested assumption and reports a single voluntary share
refuses to give any split because unknowns exist

cases.prompt: Accounts using the reporting feature churn 40% less. Should we push everyone to use reporting?
cases.setup: Feature usage was measured over each account's full lifetime.
expect_pass: identifies the observation-window artefact: churned accounts had less time to adopt anything, so lifetime-measured adoption correlates with tenure, which correlates with retention
specifies the correction: measure usage in a fixed early window, such as the first 30 days, for every account
states that even after correction the relationship is correlational, because early adopters were more engaged already
does not endorse the push as a retention lever without a test, and names the test
still reports the corrected comparison if the data allows it, rather than only objecting
expect_fail: endorses pushing the feature as a retention intervention on this evidence
reports the 40% figure with no window correction

cases.prompt: Plot 12-month retention curves for every cohort including this year's.
cases.setup: The three most recent cohorts are 3, 5 and 7 months old.
expect_pass: leaves the unreached months absent for the young cohorts rather than carrying the last value forward or filling zero
states that zero and missing are different states and that a carried-forward value reads as excellent retention
sizes every cohort in the output
compares cohorts only at matched ages, and says which comparison is actually available
applies the small-n floor, reporting counts rather than a jagged percentage curve for any thin cohort
expect_fail: extends young cohorts to month 12 by carrying values forward
plots a thin cohort as a percentage curve without its size

cases.prompt: This enterprise account churned and the reason field says price increase. Write the post-mortem.
cases.setup: Usage declined steadily for six months before cancellation. The price increase was announced five weeks before the cancellation.
expect_pass: reports both: the recorded reason and the six-month usage decline that preceded the price announcement
states which is the stronger evidence and why, since the decline began long before the price change existed
frames price as plausibly the proximate trigger for a decision about value made earlier, rather than dismissing the reason field outright
notes the disagreement is itself a finding about the reason-capture process, worth reporting if it recurs
does not write the post-mortem as a pricing failure
expect_fail: accepts the reason field and writes up a pricing failure
declares the reason field simply wrong with no account of why it was recorded
